blocks.text: Now we must say what الفنك [al-fanak] alphenec is, the word by which, as we said, other Arabs rendered the Hebrew שפן saphan. Gabriel Sionita, in the Geographia Nubiensis, Clim. 1, section 1, translates it white weasel. Golius renders it mustela foenaria [hay weasel], commonly fovina. That most learned man thought that فنك [fanak] phenec alludes to foenum [hay] and that fovina is named from foenum, whereas it takes its name from the French word for beech. For Giggeius, فنك [fanak] phenec is a certain most useful beast, from whose skin fur garments are obtained. But it is better to hear the Arabs themselves. Abenbitar: الفنك حر طيب الرايحة اطيب من جميع انواع الفرأء يجلب كثيرا [al-fanak ḥarr ṭayyib al-rāyiḥa aṭyab min jamīʿ anwāʿ al-farʾāʾ yujlab kathīran] [col. 1007] من الصقالبة ويشبه ان يكون في لحمه حلاوة وهو ابرد من السمور واحر من السنجاب واكثر الناس علي اختلاف اسنانهم يحتملون لبس الفنك [min al-ṣaqāliba wa-yushbih an yakūn fī laḥmih ḥalāwa wa-huwa abrad min al-sammūr wa-aḥarr min al-sinjāb wa-akthar al-nās ʿalā ikhtilāf asnānihim yaḥtamilūn libs al-fanak]: Phenec is an animal whose skin is warm and of good odour, the most fragrant of all kinds of furs. It is brought in great quantity from Secalia. Its flesh seems to be sweet. Its skin is colder than the skin of τοῦ [tou] simor, but warmer than the skin of τοῦ [tou] sungiab. It is especially customary to be clothed in this skin as age advances. Razi: الفنك والقماقم والحواصل معتدلة في الحرارة وهو مع ذلك خفيفة [al-fanak wa-al-qamāqim wa-al-ḥawāṣil muʿtadila fī al-ḥarāra wa-huwa maʿa dhālika khafīfa]: The pelts of alphenec, alkamakim and alhawasil are of moderate warmth, and moreover light. Damir: الفنك دويبة يوخذ منها الفرو قال ابن البيطار انه اطيب من جميع الفراء يجلب كثيرا من بلاد الصقلاب [al-fanak duwaybba yūkhadh minhā al-farw qāla Ibn al-Bayṭār innahu aṭyab min jamīʿ al-firāʾ yujlab kathīran min bilād al-ṣaqlāb]: Alphenec, a small animal from which fur is taken. Abenbitar said that it is the most fragrant of all furs, and that very much of it is brought from the Sclavic region. That is how it should be read above as well, not صقالية [Ṣaqāliya] Secalia. (The Sclavic region, that is, the region of the Sclavi, was formerly in European Scythia toward the western Ocean, as Simocatta attests, book 6, chapter 2.) Ibnomar Ben Abdalbar, in the book entitled غهيد [ghhyd], that is, Explanation: الفنك والسنجاب والسمور كل ذلك سبع كالثعلب وابن عرس [al-fanak wa-al-sinjāb wa-al-sammūr kull dhālika sabʿ ka-al-thaʿlab wa-ibn ʿirs]: Phenec, sungiab and simur are all wild beasts like the fox and the weasel. So they say. From this it might seem to follow that these pelts belong to species of marten. Yet الفنك [al-fanak] alphenec po[?]

[II, 417] is the Pontic mouse, that is, a species of mouse or squirrel, which Hermolaus calls the Venetian and Agricola the Finnish, after the Veneti and the Finni, peoples on the Vistula in Borussia, from whom it is brought to us for use as fur. Of these peoples Ptolemy says, in his description of Sarmatia: Παρὰ μὲν τὸν Οὐιστούλαν ποταμὸν ὑπὸ τοὺς Οὐενέδας Γύθωνες, εἶτα Φίννοι· [Para men ton Ouistoulan potamon hypo tous Ouenedas Gythōnes, eita Phinnoi]: On the Vistula river, below the Veneti, are the Gythones, then the Finni. From these Finni, I say, the Finnish mouse seems to be named, and in Arabic فنك [fanak] phenec, which the French call petigris from its size and colour ^{(4)}. But for Golius, سنجاب [sinjāb] sungiab is also the squirrel, an animal of ash-grey colour, and its skin, with which garments are lined, or rather minium (he meant, I believe, herminium [ermine]). Damir says it is an animal in the shape of a mole, larger than a mouse, living in the tops of trees, with a bluish, very soft, very beautiful skin, in which people of refinement are clothed. It is evident that a species of squirrel is being described. Simur, too, is a kind of mouse, not altogether unknown to the Greeks. Hesychius: Σίμωρ παρὰ Πάρθοις καλεῖταί τι μυὸς ἀγρίου εἶδος, οὗ ταῖς δοραῖς [Simōr para Parthois kaleitai ti myos agriou eidos, hou tais dorais] [col. 1008] χρῶνται πρὸς χιτῶνας· [chrōntai pros chitōnas]: Among the Parthians a certain species of wild mouse is called simor, whose skins are used for garments. For others, simur is the marten. Damir says that it is an animal similar to a cat, or, in the opinion of some, النمس [al-nims] to a ferret, whose skin so excels in softness, lightness, warmth and beauty that kings and magnates are clothed in it. I could add much more about both pelts, drawn from the books of the Arabs. But to explain each of these points more precisely is not a matter for our leisure, and it contributes little to the present subject.
Among the Greeks there is a similar inconsistency in explaining the word שפן saphan.
1. There are those who render it λαγωοὺς [lagōous], as the Vulgate translator renders it little hares: this we have already examined above.

2. There have been those who preferred the hyena, such as Clement of Alexandria, book 2 of the Paedagogus, chapter 10, where he introduces Moses saying: Οὐκ ἔδεσαι τὸν λαγὼν, οὐδὲ τὴν ὕαιναν [Ouk edesai ton lagōn, oude tēn hyainan], You shall not eat the hare, nor the hyena, that is, הארנבת והשפן. Similar to this is what we read in the Epistle of Barnabas: Ἀλλὰ καὶ δασύποδα οὐ φάγῃ [Alla kai dasypoda ou phagē], But neither shall you eat the hare. And shortly after: Ἀλλὰ οὐδὲ τὴν ὕαιναν φάγῃ [Alla oude tēn hyainan phagē], for which the old version has But neither shall you eat the beast. I would prefer beluum or belbum [hyena]. For so Julius Capitolinus writes in the third Gordian: Under Gordian there were at Rome XXXII elephants, X elks, X tigers, LX tame lions, [II, 418] XXX tame leopards, X belbi, that is, hyenas. Yet in the Glossary of Philoxenus: Ὕαινα· ζῶον [Hyaina: zōon], bellua [beast].
